subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
passage:
Dear Rafiq Sir,
Here is our team update. We have split the work by strengths. Tarun does the wiring, because the soldering is always the neatest. Ishita writes the code. I am doing the documentation and will present to the judges, since I like explaining. But we don't work in separate boxes: every Friday we meet for twenty minutes, and each person explains their part in five minutes, and the rest ask questions. That way we can all describe the whole robot, even the parts we didn't build. Last Friday Ishita spotted a wiring idea from Tarun's explanation that saved a wire. Could you please look at our documentation draft on Monday?
Yours sincerely,
Neelam

qa.q: Who handles the code on the team?
How does Neelam seem to feel about the team's plan?
qa.a: Neelam seems confident and positive, since the plan uses everyone's strengths and still keeps shared understanding.

qa.q: What could the team do if one member is absent on the event day?
qa.a: The Friday explanations mean someone else already understands that part and could step in.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel about doing the wiring?
qa.a: Tarun is probably proud to be trusted with the work Tarun does best.

grounding: One student handles wiring, another coding, another documentation and presentation, and they swap ideas at weekly meetings.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
passage: You want to know how three of us built a sorting robot in eight weeks without a single big fight? Honestly, it was the roles. I'm Yamini, I'm the talker, so I took the documentation and the presentation. Hrithik has hands like a watch-repairer, so the wiring was his. Fatima writes code the way I write messages, fast and neat, so she took the program. But here's what we did right: every Saturday morning we met for one hour, and each person had to explain their part to the other two. I learned what a pull-up resistor is. Hrithik learned why judges care about a clean diagram. When Fatima was down with fever before the demo, Hrithik and I could still run the code and explain it. Splitting the work is good. Splitting the understanding is not.

qa.q: When did the three meet each week?
qa.a: Every Saturday morning, for one hour.

qa.q: How does Yamini feel about the team's roles?
qa.a: Yamini sounds proud and confident, pleased that each person's strength had a place and that the Saturday meetings kept everyone in the loop.

qa.q: What else could the team do if a weekly meeting had to be skipped?
qa.a: Each person could send a short voice note explaining what changed, so the shared understanding doesn't slip.

qa.q: How was Hrithik affected when Fatima fell ill?
qa.a: Because of the weekly explanations, Hrithik could still run and explain the code, so the illness didn't leave him stuck.

grounding: Shows a team giving wiring, coding and presentation to the members best suited, while weekly meetings keep everyone understanding every part.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
passage: Every Sunday for two months, Tejas's team took over our dining table, and I got to watch from the sofa. I'm his younger sibling; I'm not in the club. Tejas did the wiring. He'd sit with a magnifier, soldering tiny joints without talking. Vandana did the coding on her laptop, humming. Their third member, Ashwin, did the poster and the report, and he kept asking them both, "Explain it like I'm ten." Some Sundays that seemed to annoy Vandana. She'd sigh before answering. But one day Ashwin's question made her stop mid-sentence, change a number in her code, and say, "Oh. That's the bug." At the competition, Ashwin explained the circuit to the judges better than Tejas could have. I can't say what each of them felt, but their robot looked like one person had built it.

qa.q: What might Vandana have felt when Ashwin kept asking questions?
qa.a: Vandana may have felt a little annoyed, sighing before answering, until one question helped her spot the bug.

qa.q: What else could keep the team's shared understanding strong?
qa.a: They could rotate who explains at each meeting, so everyone practises describing every part, not only their own.

qa.q: How does Tejas's younger sibling see the team's work?
qa.a: The sibling can't be sure what each felt, but sees three people with separate jobs whose robot looked like one person built it.

grounding: Illustrates a team splitting wiring, coding and documentation by strength and swapping explanations each week so understanding stays shared.
